segments.voice: Yesterday, in their own words where they exist: Maitreyi, offered a share of the property, asking what she'd do with what can't make her immortal. Did you ask her question of something you wanted? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-nine.

At the end of a hymn, the poet signs her name. Some Tamil hymns close this way, with the singer's name set into the last verse. This poet doesn't sign as a saint, or a lady, or a devotee. She signs as a pey, a ghoul, the kind of gaunt spirit said to haunt the burning grounds. The pey of Karaikkal. Earlier on this path we met her at her own door, giving away a mango. Today, on the last day of this season of women, we hear the name she gave herself.
screen: `A POET SIGNS HER NAME.` → `NOT A SAINT: A GHOUL.` → `THE PEY OF KARAIKKAL.`

segments.voice: Start with the story her tradition tells, in the Periya Puranam, the book of the lives of the Shaiva saints. Her name was Punitavati, a merchant's wife in Karaikkal. After the mango, her husband grew afraid of her and left. So she asked Shiva to take away the beauty she had kept for him, and give her the body of a pey instead, a body of bones and sinew, fit only for praising him. The story says she then went to Shiva's mountain, walking on her hands so her feet wouldn't touch its holy ground, and that Shiva, seeing her, called her Mother. That's why she's known as Karaikkal Ammaiyar, the mother of Karaikkal. Now her own words, in paraphrase. Her hymns picture Shiva dancing at night in the cremation ground, with flames, ash, and owls, and ghouls dancing around him. And there among them is the singer herself. She names herself in the closing verse as the pey of Karaikkal, the one who sings these words. In another poem she says, in paraphrase, that from the time she was born and learned to speak, her love was for his feet. So two names sit side by side. Mother is the name the story says Shiva gave her. Ghoul is the name she gave herself. She didn't hide the bones; she signed with them. Her hymns are kept in the Tirumurai, the same sacred collection that holds the Tevaram. And that closes this season. Sita, Draupadi, Kunti, Gandhari, Savitri, Damayanti and Shakuntala in the epics. Andal, Mirabai, Akka and Lalla in the songs. Gargi and Maitreyi in the Upanishad. And a woman who chose her own strange name.
screen: `PUNITAVATI ASKS FOR A NEW BODY` · `SHIVA CALLS HER MOTHER` · `SHE SIGNS AS THE PEY OF KARAIKKAL` · `A SEASON OF WOMEN, CLOSED`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the name you'd sign. Sit, and let the breath slow. Notice the names other people use for you: a title, a role, a nickname, someone's mother or son or boss. Let them pass by, one at a time. Then ask quietly: if I signed my own name at the end of a song about what I love most, what would I call myself? Don't polish it. Let it be strange if it's strange. Rest with that name for the sit. If you pray, you can offer that name to God. The bell holds the time.
In their own words, where they exist. Today, Karaikkal Ammaiyar, called Mother in the story, who signed her own hymns as the pey of Karaikkal. Today's word.
Your line: in their own words where they exist. Today, notice one name someone gives you, and one you'd give yourself, and let both stand. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Tamil Shaivas honor Karaikkal Ammaiyar among the Nayanars; her hymns are sung as part of the Tirumurai, and her image is found in Shiva temples, seated near the dancing Shiva.
